verdicts.why: B does much more of the core cleanup the brief asks for: rumble drops to -53 dB against A's -21 dB, which fails that check, hum prominence falls to 8.3 dB against A's 17.7 dB, and the soft passages are evened out better (dip gap -1.0 vs -3.2). B does over-process, though. It runs two strong denoise passes at nr=30, uses a gate, applies dynaudnorm at g=15 and mixes in pink noise, and its fidelity falls below the input (0.774 vs A's 0.813), so it may sound slightly underwater. A is the gentler and more robust script, but it leaves audible rumble and hum, which is the bigger failure for a file that has to be ready to post.

A actually removes the air-handler rumble (-53 dB relative vs B's -21 dB, which fails) and gets the hum far lower (8.3 vs 17.7 dB prominence), while also evening out the soft lean-away passages much better (dip gap -1.0 vs -3.2 dB). A's two strong afftdn passes, gate and added pink noise are heavier-handed and cost some fidelity (0.774 vs 0.813), so it may sound a little processed. Still, B's gentler chain leaves two of the brief's three named noise problems clearly audible, so it isn't ready to post.

B sets the music level from measured LUFS of both files and ducks with a gain curve built from silencedetect. That gives clean, deep ducking (20.9 dB duck, 21 dB voice-over-music), lets the music rise in the gaps between sentences, and scores higher on voice fidelity (0.926 vs 0.872). A uses a hard-coded -14 dB music gain and a fixed-threshold sidechain compressor at ratio 12. The ducking is shallower (13.4 dB), it is more likely to pump on breaths and word tails, and the -14 dB offset only works for this one pair of files. B also hits the brief's -1 dBTP limit exactly, while A undershoots it at -1.5.

A measures the voice and music loudness to set the bed level, then builds a duck curve from silence detection that ramps down just before each sentence and comes back up in the gaps. That gives a deeper duck (20.9 vs 13.4 dB), much better voice-to-music separation (21.0 vs 12.3 dB) and higher voice fidelity (0.926 vs 0.872). B uses a fixed -14 dB music trim and a sidechain compressor at ratio 12 with a set threshold, which only suits these particular files, can pump, and keeps the voice less clear of the music, even though both pass every check and hit -14 LUFS at 30 s.

A actually removes the hum (prominence drops from 29.9 to 7.1 dB because its notches cover both the 50 Hz and 60 Hz families), while B's 60 Hz-only EQ leaves it at 27.3 dB, almost untouched. A also evens out the lean-away dips (gap of -0.8 dB against B's -5.4 dB) and hits -18.0 LUFS exactly, and it checks its own output. The cost is A's dynaudnorm: it pushes noise up in the pauses, leaves the rumble barely reduced, and lowers fidelity (0.755 against B's 0.815), so B sounds cleaner between phrases but misses two core parts of the brief.

A's filter graph sends the music back into the final amix instead of the voice, so the voice is basically missing from the output (vmr -73.6 dB, fidelity 0.31, no ducking), and it fails half the checks; its music also fades before 30 s instead of after a swell. B detects sentence gaps to build a smooth duck that rises between lines and after her last word, sets the music level from measured voice loudness, and uses two-pass linear loudnorm to land at -13.9 LUFS / -1.0 dBTP, passing all 12 checks.

B never mixes the voice into the output. Its sidechaincompress output is only the ducked music, which then gets mixed back with the music, so the voice checks fail (vmr -73.6 dB, fidelity 0.31, no ducking) and the brief's main purpose is lost. A finds the speech spans from the file itself, ducks the music about 25 dB under her with gentle ramps, brings it back up in the gaps and after her last word, ends cleanly with the 2-second fade, and uses two-pass linear loudnorm to land on -14 LUFS / -1 dBTP, passing all 12 checks.
